The Antolia bream Acanthobrama thisbeae is a freshwater cyprinid endemic to a restricted drainage basin in western Anatolia, where it occupies lentic and slow-flowing lotic habitats. Field surveys indicate that the species attains a maximum adult total length of 26.1 centimeters [Li = 26.1 centimeters], a figure derived from extensive gill-net sampling campaigns across multiple seasons. Examination of ovarian development in dissected females reveals that the onset of gonadal recrudescence, marking the transition to sexual maturity, occurs at a total length of 13 centimeters [Lp = 13 centimeters]. This threshold length corresponds to the point at which vitellogenic oocytes first become macroscopically visible, a criterion commonly used to define the attainment of puberty in cyprinid fishes. At this stage of reproductive development, the calculated somatic wet weight of an individual is 22.5 grams [Wwp = 22.5 grams], a value derived from the species-specific length-weight relationship. Above this size threshold, individuals are considered capable of participating in the annual spawning aggregation.

Reproductive output in Acanthobrama thisbeae is closely tied to the body size of the spawning female. The maximum asymptotic wet weight observed in the population reaches 107 grams [Wwi = 107 grams], a value that characterizes the heaviest individuals from the oldest year classes present in the lake. This ultimate mass is a reliable predictor of fecundity, as gravid females approaching this size class possess the largest ovarian reserves. In contrast, the earliest stages of the life cycle begin with a wet weight at birth of approximately 0.0082 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0082 grams], which is the calculated mass of the freshly hatched prolarva, derived from an egg diameter measurement. This neonatal mass is consistent with the small, pelagic eggs typical of many cyprinids that broadcast spawn in open water. The substantial increase in body mass from the prolarval stage to the asymptotic adult weight underscores a pronounced ontogenetic trajectory, with a growth coefficient that shifts notably around the onset of sexual maturation.

Embryonic development and the timing of hatching are modulated by ambient water temperature, a critical abiotic factor for spring-spawning cyprinids. At a constant incubation temperature of 22 °C [T = 22 °C], the hatching event, marking the transition from the chorionate embryo to the free-swimming yolk-sac larva, occurs after approximately 13 days [ab = approximately 13 days]. This incubation period was recorded under controlled laboratory conditions using fertilized eggs sourced from wild-caught broodstock. The lecithotrophic yolk-sac larva, or alevin, relies entirely on endogenous yolk reserves during these initial days post-eclosion, a non-feeding phase that lasts until the mouth opens and the digestive tract becomes patent. At this same ambient temperature of 22 °C [T = 22 °C], the maximum documented longevity for the species is 2,920 days [am = 2,920 days], an estimate derived from mark-recapture studies and validated by otolith annulus counts from the oldest individuals in the sample. This lifespan places Acanthobrama thisbeae among the longer-lived species within its regional fish assemblage.

The reproductive life history of Acanthobrama thisbeae, when framed within a comparative context, reveals a strategy that balances moderate longevity with a protracted but regular spawning schedule. The total lifespan of 2,920 days [am = 2,920 days] at 22 °C [T = 22 °C] includes several years of reproductive activity following the attainment of puberty at 13 centimeters [Lp = 13 centimeters]. Females achieving the adult body mass at the pubertal length of 22.5 grams [Wwp = 22.5 grams] are estimated to produce a modest number of oocytes per season. The energetic investment per offspring is low, favoring a strategy of high fecundity at each spawning event because the calculated wet weight at birth is approximately 0.0082 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0082 grams]. The ultimate wet weight of 107 grams [Wwi = 107 grams] represents the upper bound of somatic investment, and such individuals contribute disproportionately to the next generation by virtue of their larger ovarian mass.

Ecologically, the life history parameters of Acanthobrama thisbeae align with those of a zooplanktivorous, iteroparous cyprinid adapted to temperate lacustrine conditions. The age at hatching of roughly 13 days [ab = roughly 13 days] at 22 °C [T = 22 °C] synchronizes larval emergence with the spring zooplankton bloom, ensuring adequate prey availability for the exotrophic larva. The total length at puberty of 13 centimeters [Lp = 13 centimeters] represents a size refuge from gape-limited piscivores, a selective pressure that likely shapes the maturation schedule. The ultimate total length of 26.1 centimeters [Li = 26.1 centimeters] is not uncommon among regional leuciscids, yet the maximum longevity of 2,920 days [am = 2,920 days] is somewhat extended relative to similar-sized congeners, possibly reflecting the relatively stable, low-predation environment of the species' endemic lake at a temperature of 22 °C [T = 22 °C].
